## Digital Marketing Agency in Pune: How to Research Your Competitors' Ads for Free Using the Meta Ad Library and Google Ads Transparency Center

You can see most of what your competitors are advertising on Facebook, Instagram and Google without paying for a tool, and you can do it in an afternoon. Meta publishes an Ad Library of ads currently running across its platforms, and Google publishes an Ads Transparency Center showing the ads an advertiser has run. A good digital marketing agency in Pune uses both before it writes a single advert for a new client, because they answer practical questions: who is actually advertising in your market, what are they offering, how long have they kept a particular ad running, and where are you different. This guide shows you how to run that research yourself, what the data can and cannot tell you, and how to turn it into a better campaign without copying anyone.

The method is deliberately modest. Public ad libraries show what is being said, not what is working, and they do not show competitors' budgets, conversion rates or profit. Used honestly, they are a cheap way to avoid obvious mistakes and spot gaps. Used carelessly, they lead small businesses to copy a rival's offer without understanding the rival's economics. We will cover both sides.

## What these free tools actually show

Both libraries exist for transparency, not for marketing intelligence, so their coverage differs and changes over time. Treat the descriptions below as a starting point and confirm the current features in each tool's help pages.

| Question | Meta Ad Library | Google Ads Transparency Center |
|---|---|---|
| Where does it show ads? | Ads active on Meta technologies such as Facebook and Instagram | Ads served by an advertiser across Google's ad surfaces, including Search, YouTube and Display |
| Can I search by advertiser? | Yes, by Page name or keyword | Yes, by advertiser name or website domain |
| Can I see the ad creative? | Yes: image, video and text, with the platforms where it runs | Yes: the creative formats shown, filtered by format and region |
| Does it show spend and reach? | Not for ordinary commercial ads in India; fuller data is limited to certain categories and regions | No spend data for ordinary ads |
| Does it show targeting? | No detailed targeting for ordinary commercial ads | No detailed targeting |
| Does it show results? | No | No |

TODO: confirm against the current Meta Ad Library and Google Ads Transparency Center help pages what is displayed for commercial ads in India, including date ranges and whether inactive ads remain visible, before presenting this table to a client as final.

The most important row is the last one. Neither tool shows how well an ad performed. That limitation shapes everything that follows.

## Before you start: decide the question

Aimless browsing wastes time, and it makes every competitor look like a genius. Before you open either tool, write down one to three questions. Useful examples:

- Which businesses actually advertise for my main service in Pune, and which of them are just noise?
- What offers do they lead with: price, speed, guarantee, free consultation, financing?
- Which claims do they all make, and what claim could I make that none of them do?
- Are they sending people to a landing page, a WhatsApp chat, a lead form or the home page?
- Which formats do they use: single images, carousels, short video, text-only search ads?

Also decide who counts as a competitor. Include direct rivals, but remember that your customer's real alternatives may differ from the businesses you think of as competitors. A coaching class competes with other classes and with online platforms; a wedding photographer competes with other photographers and with the relative who owns a good camera. Add two or three of each type.

## Step by step: the Meta Ad Library

### 1. Open the library and choose the country

Go to the Meta Ad Library (search for "Meta Ad Library" and use the official facebook.com page) and choose India as the country. Pick the "All ads" category for a business search. Some versions of the interface ask you to choose the ad type first; for ordinary commercial advertisers the all-ads option is the one to use.

### 2. Search by name first, keyword second

Type a competitor's business name and choose their Page from the suggestions. You will see the ads currently running for that Page. Then try keywords such as "web design Pune", "interior designer Pune" or "dental implants", with the country set to India. Keyword searches look for words in the ad text, and they surface advertisers you had not thought of.

### 3. Record what you see

For each competitor, note in a spreadsheet:

- the main offer and the headline;
- the call to action button (Learn More, Send WhatsApp message, Sign Up, Call Now);
- the format (image, video, carousel);
- the language, since many Pune advertisers mix English, Marathi and Hindi;
- the start date shown for each ad;
- the number of different ads running at once;
- where the ad leads, which you can find by clicking through as a normal visitor.

Take screenshots with the date, as ads disappear when advertisers stop them.

### 4. Look at ad duration with care

Each ad shows the date it started running. An ad that has run for many months is sometimes a sign that the advertiser is happy with it, because a business that loses money on an ad usually stops it. But this is only a hint. An advertiser may leave an ad running through neglect, may be funded by a different goal such as brand awareness, or may be running a large budget that masks poor efficiency. Treat long-running ads as hypotheses worth testing, not as proof of success.

### 5. Count the variations

If a competitor runs six ads with the same offer and different pictures, they are probably testing creative. If they run one ad for a year, they may not be testing at all. The pattern tells you how seriously they take paid social, which is useful when you plan your own testing. Our guide to [Meta Ads creative testing](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-meta-ads-creative-testing-2026) explains how to run a fair test.

## Step by step: the Google Ads Transparency Center

### 1. Search by advertiser or domain

Open the Google Ads Transparency Center (adstransparency.google.com) and search for a competitor's name or website. Choose the region India so that you see the ads relevant to your market. The center lists the ads the advertiser has run and lets you filter by format and by time period.

### 2. Check the verified advertiser name

Google verifies advertisers, and the name shown is the legal or verified name, which may differ from the brand customers know. This matters in two ways. It helps you identify who is really behind a brand, and it can show that several similar-looking competitors are one company.

### 3. Study the creatives, not the keywords

The transparency center shows the ads, but it does not show which search terms triggered them or what the advertiser bid. For keyword ideas you need other sources, which we cover below. What you do get is the wording of each advertiser's headlines and descriptions, which reveals their positioning: price-led, trust-led, speed-led or location-led.

### 4. Look at the landing pages

Click through to the pages the ads lead to. Compare them with your own on the following points:

- Does the headline match the promise in the ad?
- How many fields does the form ask for?
- Is there a WhatsApp or call option on mobile?
- Does the page show proof such as named clients, ratings or certifications, and is that proof believable?
- How fast does it load on a phone with an average connection?

This is often the most valuable part of the exercise, because a weak landing page is the easiest gap to beat. If yours needs work, our article on [landing pages versus homepages for ads](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-landing-page-vs-homepage-ads-2026) shows what to change.

## Other free sources that complete the picture

The ad libraries show ads, but a full picture of the market needs a few more inputs, most of which are free.

- **Your own Search Console data.** It shows which queries already bring you impressions, so you know where you stand organically before paying for clicks. See our guide to [keyword research and search intent](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-keyword-research-search-intent-mapping-2026).
- **Google Ads Keyword Planner.** If you have a Google Ads account, it gives ranges for search volume and suggested bid ranges. These are estimates and should be treated as direction, not forecast.
- **Auction Insights.** Once you run Google Ads campaigns, the Auction Insights report shows which other advertisers appear in the same auctions, with measures such as impression share and overlap rate. It describes real competitors in your own auctions rather than guessed ones.
- **Searching like a customer.** Search your main phrases on a phone, in Pune, in an incognito window, and record who appears in the ads, the map listings and the organic results. Results vary by location and by person, so repeat at different times.
- **Competitors' websites and Business Profiles.** Their pricing pages, service lists, review counts and response style tell you how they position themselves. Our guide to [local SEO and the Google map pack](/blog/local-seo-google-map-pack-pune-2026) explains what to compare on profiles.
- **Social profiles.** Check whether they post regularly and how they answer comments and enquiries.

## Turning the research into decisions

Collecting screenshots is the easy part. The value comes from asking what the evidence means for your campaign.

### Build a simple comparison grid

Create a table with competitors in rows and these columns: main offer, price signal, proof used, call to action, landing destination, creative style and anything unusual. Fill it in from your screenshots. After four to six competitors, patterns appear. Perhaps all of them lead with a free consultation, none show a price, and only one offers WhatsApp contact.

### Look for crowded and empty ground

Crowded ground is where everyone makes the same promise: "best quality", "trusted by many", "affordable". Your ad will disappear into the crowd unless you say something specific. Empty ground is where no one speaks: perhaps nobody shows a fixed-price package, a delivery timeline or a clear explanation of what is included. A specific claim you can actually keep is often better than a louder version of a claim everyone makes.

### Decide what to test

Turn each finding into a testable hypothesis, such as "a visible starting price will produce more qualified enquiries than a free consultation offer", and test it with a small budget. Our [testing budget framework for Google Ads and Meta Ads](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-ads-meta-ads-testing-budget-2026) shows how to size a test without overspending.

### Judge on qualified leads

Whichever idea you test, judge it by qualified enquiries and customers, not clicks. A competitor's ad may attract many cheap leads that never buy, and copying its format would import the same problem. Our article on [lead quality and offline conversions](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-lead-quality-offline-conversions-2026) explains how to feed real outcomes back into the platforms.

## A worked example: an interior designer in Pune

Consider a hypothetical interior design studio in Pune that wants more enquiries for two-bedroom apartment interiors. The owner spends two hours on the research and finds the following, which is illustrative and not data from any real business:

- Several competitors run image carousels of finished homes with the offer "free design consultation".
- Most lead to a form asking for six fields, and few mention a timeline.
- One competitor mentions a fixed completion period in the ad; none state a price range.
- Most calls to action are "Get Quote", and only one offers a WhatsApp chat.
- Competitors' landing pages often load slowly on mobile and hide the contact number below the fold.

The studio decides on two tests: an ad that states a typical completion period and a starting-price range with the actual limits of what it includes, and a landing page with a three-field form and a WhatsApp option above the fold. It runs both against its current ad with a modest budget for four weeks and compares cost per qualified enquiry, not cost per click. The research did not decide the outcome; it gave the studio two sensible questions to test.

## Ethics, rules and the lines not to cross

Competitor research is normal practice, but several lines should not be crossed.

- **Do not copy creative.** Reusing a rival's images, videos or text can breach copyright and platform policies, and it makes your brand look derivative.
- **Do not impersonate or confuse.** Ads must not suggest that you are another business. Check the advertising rules of each platform before using a competitor's name in anything public.
- **Be careful with competitor trademarks.** Bidding on a rival's brand as a keyword is a separate, contested practice with its own platform policy and legal risk. Take advice before doing it, and do not use their name in your ad text without checking the policy. TODO: confirm the current Google Ads trademark policy for Indian advertisers before recommending any competitor-brand strategy to a client.
- **Respect privacy.** The libraries show ads, not people. Do not try to identify or contact individuals who interacted with an ad.
- **Follow Indian advertising standards.** The Advertising Standards Council of India has guidelines on misleading claims and influencer disclosures; our article on [ASCI influencer guidelines](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-asci-influencer-guidelines-2026) covers one part. Make claims you can substantiate.
- **Do not collect data by scraping.** Use the tools as intended. Automated scraping of the libraries may breach their terms.

## Common mistakes when researching competitors

1. **Assuming long-running ads are winners.** Duration is a hint, not proof of profit.
2. **Copying the biggest advertiser.** A larger business has different margins, brand awareness and budget; its tactics may not suit you.
3. **Ignoring the landing page.** The ad is half the story; the page decides whether the click becomes an enquiry.
4. **Researching once.** Markets change, especially around festivals and peak seasons. Re-check quarterly. Our [festival-season campaign calendar](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-festival-season-campaign-calendar-2026) shows how seasons change advertiser behaviour.
5. **Forgetting non-obvious competitors.** Marketplaces, aggregators and do-it-yourself tools often take the customers you think you are losing to a rival agency.
6. **Researching without a goal.** Without a question, you collect screenshots and decide nothing.

## What an agency should do with this research

If you hire a digital marketing agency in Pune, competitor research is a reasonable thing to ask for in the first month. A useful deliverable is short: a comparison grid, three to five observations about gaps and crowded claims, and a prioritised list of tests with a budget. Be wary of a thick report that lists competitors' ads without explaining what to do differently. Ask which hypotheses it will test first, how it will measure success and when it will review the results. Our guide to [retainer deliverables and reporting](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-retainer-deliverables-reporting-2026) explains what a sensible monthly report contains.

## A one-afternoon plan

1. **Hour one:** write your three questions, list six competitors including one alternative type, and search each in both libraries. Screenshot and record.
2. **Hour two:** click through to landing pages on a phone and record form length, speed, contact options and proof.
3. **Hour three:** search your main phrases as a Pune customer in incognito mode and record who appears in ads, maps and organic results.
4. **Hour four:** fill in the comparison grid, mark crowded and empty ground, and write down two or three testable hypotheses.
5. **After:** run one small test, judge it on qualified enquiries and repeat the research next quarter.

**Related reading:** Competitor research also shows how rivals handle local reviews; for your own profile, read [how to get Google reviews legitimately and respond to them](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-google-business-profile-reviews-2026/).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can I see how much a competitor spends on Facebook or Google ads?

For ordinary commercial ads in India, the public libraries do not show spend, reach or results. They show which ads are running and, in some cases, when they started. Estimates of competitor spend from third-party tools are guesses, so treat them with caution.

### Is it legal to look at competitors' ads in the Ad Library?

Yes. The Meta Ad Library and Google Ads Transparency Center are published for public use. What you do with the information matters: copying creative, impersonating a rival or breaching platform policies can cause legal and account problems.

### How do I know which of my competitor's ads are working?

You cannot know from the libraries alone. Long-running ads and many variations are hints that an advertiser is satisfied, but they are not proof. The reliable way to learn what works for you is to test your own ads and judge them on qualified enquiries and sales.

### Should I bid on my competitors' brand names?

It is a contested tactic with platform policy and legal considerations, and it often draws low-quality clicks because the searcher wanted a different business. Take professional advice before trying it, and test on a small budget if you do.

### How often should I check my competitors' ads?

Quarterly is enough for most small businesses, with an extra check before major seasons such as Ganeshotsav, Diwali and the wedding period. More frequent checking tends to produce anxiety rather than decisions.
